title: The Child Born of the Virgin Is God
english: …translated, 'God with us' (Matthew 1:23). So the one who was born is God, whether you like it or not.
Nestorius says: The angel said to Joseph, 'Rise, take the child and his mother, and flee into Egypt, and stay there until I tell you' (Matthew 2:13). But he did not say, 'Take God and his mother.'

Cyril says: But the archangel Gabriel says to the Virgin, 'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who is born of you will be called Son of the Most High' (Luke 1:35).

Nestorius says: The Apostle said, 'He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant' (Philippians 2:7); that is, he put on our body, in which he advanced in wisdom and stature and grace before God and men (Luke 2:52), as the Lord's man.
Cyril says: 'Everything that is born of the flesh is flesh' (John 3:6); yet this does not do away with the wonder of the birth. For just as God begets in a manner proper to God, so…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 76, col. 252 (Dialogus cum Nestorio). The section opens mid-sentence, finishing Cyril's citation of Isaiah 7:14 begun in the previous section ('which is' + 'translated, God with us'); the gloss 'which being translated' is Matthew 1:23, so that verse is cited, with Isaiah 7:14 as the prophecy behind it.

Luke 1:35 as Cyril quotes it reads 'Son of the Most High' (υἱὸς Ὑψίστου), the wording of Luke 1:32, where the received text of 1:35 has 'Son of God'; translated as the Greek here stands, and cited to 1:35, where the rest of the quotation comes from.
Κυριακὸς ἄνθρωπος is rendered 'the Lord's man' (Latin homo dominicus), the term for the assumed man in Antiochene Christology; it is kept as a term, not smoothed away.
τίκτει θεϊκῶς: τίκτω is used here of the Father's begetting of the Son; rendered 'begets in a manner proper to God'. The sentence breaks at οὕτω ('so') and continues at the start of the next section.

John 3:6 is quoted in a slightly varied form (πᾶν τὸ γενόμενον for τὸ γεγεννημένον); translated as given. Run-together words in the print (ἀναστὰς παράλαβε, ἐκένωσε, μορφήν) are read apart; no wording is supplied.
baehrens: PG 76; CPG 5228 (Dialogus cum Nestorio) dial rem early

title: One Son, of One Substance with His Mother
english: …the Virgin too, worthy of God, bore in the flesh God the Word, who is from God.

Nestorius says: Every mother bears what is of one substance with herself. So she is not his mother unless he is of one substance with her. For how is she his mother when he is foreign to her substance?
Cyril says: We have been taught to confess one Son from the Virgin and from the Holy Spirit, of one substance with his mother as he is with the Father, as the Fathers have said.
Nestorius says: I divide the natures, but I unite the worship, since God is inseparable from the one who is seen; for this reason I do not separate the honor.
Cyril says: Whoever divides the natures speaks of two sons, and does not believe the Scripture that says, 'The Word became flesh' (John 1:14).

Nestorius says: Paul says that Jesus became the high priest and apostle of our confession, being faithful to the one who made him (Hebrews 3:1-2), and that he offered himself as a sacrifice for himself as for the people (Hebrews 5:3; 7:27); hence he is appointed high priest in the things that pertain to God (Hebrews 5:1).
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 76, col. 252 (Dialogus cum Nestorio). The section opens mid-sentence, completing 'For just as God begets in a manner proper to God, so…' from the previous section; καί is rendered 'too'. It ends at 'Christ', and Cyril's quotation of Hebrews 9:28 continues at the start of the next section ('having been offered once…'); the citation is placed here beside the opening word.
θεοπρεπής is rendered 'worthy of God' (literally 'befitting God'). τὸν ἐκ Θεοῦ Θεὸν Λόγον is rendered 'God the Word, who is from God'.

ὁμοούσιος is rendered 'of one substance' throughout, matching the Nicene term. The bracketed editorial variant [ξοδ. τὸ ἀλλότριον ὑπάρχον] does not change the sense and is not translated. ἀχώριστος is rendered 'inseparable'.

Cyril's sentence begins with an accusative ἡμᾶς and a passive verb (ἐδιδάχθημεν); rendered by the plain sense 'We have been taught'. 'The Fathers' here means the earlier teachers of the Church and is capitalised.

Nestorius' summary of Hebrews: 'high priest and apostle of our confession… faithful to the one who made him' follows Hebrews 3:1-2 (with the order of the two titles reversed and ἑαυτόν for αὐτόν); 'offered himself… for himself as for the people' draws on Hebrews 5:3 (the high priest offers 'for the people, so also for himself'), with the wording of Hebrews 7:27 ('offered himself'); both are cited, since 7:27 alone would point the reader to a verse that says the opposite; 'appointed… in the things that pertain to God' is Hebrews 5:1. The 'for himself as for the people' wording is kept as given, since Cyril answers it directly in the next section ('not for himself, but for the people'). Hebrews is attributed to Paul, as in the Greek.
baehrens: PG 76; CPG 5228 (Dialogus cum Nestorio) dial rem mid

title: Christ's Sacrifice and the Eucharist
english: '…having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, apart from sin' (Hebrews 9:28). And again: 'He committed no sin, and there was no deceit in his mouth' (1 Peter 2:22). And look, he himself offers himself for us. See, then: he did not offer himself up for himself, but for the people.

Nestorius says: Since he says, 'Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood will live through me, just as I live because of the Father who sent me' (John 6:56-57), what then do you eat, heretic? The divinity, or the humanity? For Christ did not say, 'Whoever eats my divinity,' but 'the flesh.'
Cyril says: For my part, I receive by faith the life-giving flesh of the life-giving Word. Hence the Savior said, 'Those who eat of this bread will never taste death' (John 6:50-51; 8:52). Those who…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 76, cols. 252-253 (Dialogus cum Nestorio). The section opens inside Cyril's quotation of Hebrews 9:28, begun at the end of the previous section ('Christ…'), and breaks off mid-sentence at οἱ ('Those who…'), where the text translated here ends.
The speaker labels {ΝΕΣΤ.} and {ΚΥΡ.} in the print mark the change of speaker: Nestorius asks the question about eating the divinity or the humanity, and Cyril answers.

ἴδε οὖν is 'See, then'. In the John 6 quotation (6:56-57), διὰ τὸν Πατέρα (accusative) is 'because of the Father'. The bread saying joins John 6:50-51 with the 'never taste death' wording of John 8:52.
τὴν τοῦ ζωοποιοῦ Λόγου ζωοποιοῦσαν σάρκα is rendered 'the life-giving flesh of the life-giving Word', keeping Cyril's repeated word.
baehrens: PG 76; CPG 5228 (Dialogus cum Nestorio) dial rem close
